summary: Brick light at the St. James harbor on Beaver Island, Lake Michigan: established 1856, tower rebuilt 1870, keeper Elizabeth Whitney Williams 1872-1884; the tower is closed.

structures.note: 34 ft from base to lantern centre (archive); fourth-order Fresnel lens still inside (LighthouseFriends)
Low tower with cracked walls by 1867, as quoted by LighthouseFriends
Torn down in the winter of 1941-42 (LighthouseFriends)

staffing.note: Last roster keeper, Ernst E. Winter, served to 1927; the 1930 census lists him as custodian (LighthouseFriends)

access.note: Owned by St. James Township; tower closed. Reached by ferry from Charlevoix and a walk from the ferry dock. The archive lists the station as not open to the public.

events.note: Congress appropriated $6,000 for a light to mark the harbor, 3 August 1854 (as quoted by LighthouseFriends)
Station established (archive year established 1856)
Brick structure erected; first lens sixth order per LighthouseFriends, fourth order per archive
Original optic: fourth-order Fresnel per archive; sixth-order per LighthouseFriends (disputed)
Lyman Granger, first keeper on the archive roster
Lighthouse Board: harbor 'but indifferently lighted', tower walls badly cracked, higher tower proposed (as quoted by LighthouseFriends)
Congress provided $5,000 for a new tower, 20 July 1868 (as quoted by LighthouseFriends)
New cylindrical brick tower with iron stairway and fourth-order lens
Fixed white changed to fixed red
Schooner Thomas Howland in distress; storm; keeper Clement Van Riper drowned trying to help her crew (memoir; year from roster)
Elizabeth Whitney Williams transferred to the new Little Traverse light at Harbor Point; that lamp first lit 25 September 1884
Coal-laden schooner A. Boody stranded in a southwest blow near the Beaver Island life-saving station (19 July 1888)
Station grounds fenced: 800 running feet of fence, four gates (Board report, fiscal 1892)
Dwelling cellar re-excavated and given a concrete floor
Last roster keeper Ernst E. Winter leaves service
Keeper's brick dwelling torn down (winter 1941-42)
Light's name officially changed to St. James Light
Light electrified
Renewable ten-year lease of the brick tower to St. James Township
Lighthouse officially awarded to St. James Township
Restoration estimate of $196,000 reported; long-term restoration unresolved

resolved_conflicts.explanation: 1856 is the first light (archive year established 1856; LighthouseFriends: brick structure erected 1856). 1870 is the present tower (archive year tower established 1870). The record's 1870 is the tower date.

notes_for_editor: (1) Lens order conflict for 1856: archive says fourth order; LighthouseFriends says sixth order. The 1870 tower's fourth-order lens is consistent across archive, LighthouseFriends and memoir. (2) Focal height: archive 37 ft above water (11.3 m); Wikipedia gives 38 ft, citing the Michigan Lighthouse Conservancy page, which 404'd and was not read. The present characteristic (record: Iso R 6s) is from the Coast Guard Light List, not read for this story; the story gives only the 1870 change from fixed white to fixed red. (3) The memoir (1905) names a Mr. Van Allen as first keeper 'when the light was first erected' and a Mr. Loaney as second; both are undated and not on the archive roster. The memoir's 'Beaver Island lighthouse at the head of the Island' may be a different light (the Beaver Island Head light is on the south end). Not added to the roster; flagged. (4) The Lighthouse Board fiscal 1891-92 and 1895 reports are in the corpus and cited by printed page (confirmed by the report indexes). The Board's 1867 report and the 1854 and 1868 appropriations are second-hand (LighthouseFriends) and should be checked in the primaries; they are not in the corpus. (5) Thomas Howland storm: 1872 comes from the archive roster (Van Riper 1869-1872) and LighthouseFriends; Chronicling America searches for the schooner and Van Riper in 1872 found nothing relevant, so the exact date is unconfirmed. (6) A. Boody stranding dated 19 July 1888: the report is for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1889, so July falls in 1888; printed page 81 from the OCR head. The life-saving station is not in data/stations and is not linked. (7) Beaver Island Head (a different light, 'Beaver Island, Michigan' in the Board reports, with steam sirens from December 1890) is excluded throughout. (8) NRHP correction (2026-10-27): reference 78001495 is the 1978 nomination for the 'Beaver Island Light Station', which describes the Beaver Island Head light (1851 construction, decommissioned 1962; Wikidata Q4878099 'Beaver Island Head Light' carries the same reference). It is not the St. James light. The earlier sentence giving this light an NRHP record was removed and source 8 dropped. Whether the St. James light has any NRHP listing was not established. (9) The Whiskey Point restoration figures come from the Beaver Island Archive, which summarises the Beaver Beacon (2011); the archive says the estimate is not evidence of funding. (10) Mrs. Granger and Elizabeth Whitney's pre-1872 unofficial work at the lamp are in prose, not the roster. (11) Winter's 1927 end is the roster date; the 'automated 1927' figure in Wikipedia is not cited. (12) No new photos. (13) Verification 2026-10-27: the 1895 concrete-floor entry is at scan page 335 (printed page 128 by the report's index), not scan page 421 as first cited. The Whiskey Point material is the Beaver Island Archive's summary of the Beaver Beacon (April and October 2011), so the story footnotes it that way; the archive's own evidence limit (the estimate is not evidence of funding) is kept. The memoir gives no year for the Thomas Howland storm; the 1872 date rests on the roster's end year for Van Riper and is stated as such in the story. The A. Boody entry (scan page 89, printed page 81) is confirmed by two copies of the 1889 report. The Board's 1892 fence entry (Beaver Island Harbor, no. 1186) is confirmed as the harbor station, not Beaver Island Head.
